imfeatures

imfeatures extracts visual features from 2D images using deep learning models and traditional computer vision techniques. It combines fast R-native image descriptors with optional Python-backed deep-learning features.

What it does

  • Edge entropy: compute_edge_entropy() measures first-order oriented-edge entropy and pairwise edge entropy across distance ranges. It works on grayscale matrices or image paths and does not require Python.
  • Saliency-modulated entropy: compute_saliency_features() weights image edges by an aligned heat map and returns controls and support diagnostics. Separate functions describe map concentration and multiscale spatial entropy.
  • Multiscale color entropy: image_mse() computes mean multiscale entropy for the H, S, and V channels of an imager::cimg image. This is also R-native.
  • VGG-16 features: extract_vgg_features() extracts pooled low-, mid-, high-, or semantic-tier VGG-16 activations. im_features() and im_feature_sim() expose lower-level layer selection and similarity matrices.
  • Feature hierarchies: extract_feature_hierarchy() returns named stage blocks with per-stage poolers. fit_hierarchy_transform() then compresses those blocks and applies ordered innovations that can be reused on new images.
  • Model zoo features: im_features_tv() uses Python thingsvision for torchvision, timm, SSL, CLIP, and related models.
  • Vision-language features: caption_features() can generate captions and optional caption embeddings through ellmer providers.

Install 

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("bbuchsbaum/imfeatures")

Python is only needed for the deep-learning and vision-language backends. The entropy functions can be used after installing the R package.

Quick Examples

Compute edge entropy for a grayscale matrix:

library(imfeatures)

set.seed(1)
img <- matrix(runif(96 * 96), nrow = 96)

edge <- compute_edge_entropy(img)
edge[, c("entropy", "pentropy_20_80", "pentropy_80_160", "pentropy_160_240")]

Weight image structure by an aligned saliency heat map:

library(imfeatures)
img <- outer(1:24, 1:24, function(x, y) sin(x * .6) + cos(y * .4))
xy <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = nrow(img))
saliency <- outer(xy, xy, function(x, y) exp(-4 * (x^2 + y^2)))
attention <- compute_saliency_features(
  img, saliency, representation = "weights", pairwise = FALSE,
  filter_length = 7L, gabor_bins = 8L
)
attention$features[, c("control", "first_order", "effective_fraction")]
#>             control first_order effective_fraction
#> 1          observed    2.852257          0.4728147
#> 2        unweighted    2.879718          1.0000000
#> 3       centre_bias    2.925043          0.7762660
#> 4        flip_axis1    2.852257          0.4728147
#> 5        flip_axis2    2.852257          0.4728147
#> 6         rotate180    2.852257          0.4728147
#> 7          rotate90    2.852257          0.4728147
#> 8         rotate270    2.852257          0.4728147
#> 9 donor_unavailable          NA                 NA

# Pairwise features are enabled by default; pairwise = FALSE is a cheaper start.
# Use representation = "log_density" for natural-log density outputs.
spatial <- saliency_multiscale_entropy(saliency, "weights")
spatial$summary
#>   scale_index   scale block_pixels H_location KL_uniform effective_fraction
#> 1           1 0.03125            1   8.089272  1.0806533          0.4728147
#> 2           2 0.06250            2   6.113612  1.0599181          0.4796593
#> 3           3 0.12500            3   4.979771  1.0261918          0.4910046
#> 4           4 0.25000            6   3.160796  0.8626650          0.5499451
#> 5           5 0.50000           12   1.710975  0.4253822          0.7609434
#>   status
#> 1     ok
#> 2     ok
#> 3     ok
#> 4     ok
#> 5     ok

The controls include unweighted edges, a declared Gaussian centre bias, and exact flips/rotations. Supply saliency_donor_assignments() and named donor maps for cross-image controls; without a donor pool those controls are explicitly unavailable. These comparisons describe model-weighted image structure and do not establish an effect of human attention. The new API uses the same geometry and validity rules in both backends. Pairwise family contrasts use common valid cells; raw unweighted contrasts describe the overall effect of weighting. See vignette("saliency-entropy") for a runnable workflow, concentration-matched controls, support diagnostics, and interpretation.

Compute multiscale HSV entropy for an imager image:

library(imfeatures)
library(imager)

img <- load.example("parrots")
image_mse(img)

Extract VGG-16 features from your own image directory:

library(imfeatures)

imgs <- list.files(
  "path/to/images",
  pattern = "\\.(jpe?g|png)$",
  full.names = TRUE,
  ignore.case = TRUE
)
stopifnot(length(imgs) >= 2)

vgg <- extract_vgg_features(imgs, tier = "mid", pooling = "avg")
dim(vgg$features)

Compute pairwise feature similarities from selected VGG-16 layers:

library(imfeatures)

sim <- im_feature_sim(
  imgs,
  layers = c("block3_conv3", "block4_conv3"),
  spatial_pooling = "avg",
  lowmem = FALSE
)

sim$layer_block3_conv3

Spatial pooling

Convolutional layers return a map per channel. Spatial pooling turns those maps into a feature vector, and decides how much the features remember about where in the image something occurred.

You want extract_feature_hierarchy() extract_vgg_features(), im_features()
One value per channel global_average_pool(), global_max_pool() "avg", "max"
Coarse location in a grid adaptive_grid_pool(ny, nx) "resize_HxW"
The average plus smooth layout contrasts dct_pool(ny, nx) –
Centre versus periphery radial_pool(breaks) –
Every position identity_pool() "none" 
# One pooling for a whole tier
vgg_3x3 <- extract_vgg_features(imgs, tier = "high", pooling = "resize_3x3")

# A pooler per stage: DCT modes for block 4, rings for block 5
spec <- vgg_hierarchy_spec(
  "vgg16",
  taps = c(b4 = "block4_conv3", b5 = "block5_conv3"),
  pooling = list(b4 = dct_pool(3, 3), b5 = radial_pool())
)
raw <- extract_feature_hierarchy(imgs, spec = spec)

vgg16_block_end_spec() is a ready-made spec with DCT pooling at the end of each block. See vignette("spatial-pooling") for what each option keeps, the resulting feature sizes, and how to choose.

Generate captions or caption embeddings when an ellmer provider is configured:

library(imfeatures)

captions <- caption_features(
  imgs,
  caption_provider = "openai",
  template = "dense",
  compute_embedding = TRUE,
  embedding_backend = "openai"
)

Python Setup

For workstation use, imfeatures_config() creates or activates the Python environment used by Keras, thingsvision, PyTorch, and open_clip:

library(imfeatures)
imfeatures_config()

If you already manage Python yourself, point reticulate at that interpreter:

library(imfeatures)
use_existing_python("/full/path/to/python")

HPC Setup

On HPC systems, avoid automatic Conda setup during package load. The usual pattern is:

Sys.setenv(IMFEATURES_SKIP_PYTHON = "TRUE")
library(imfeatures)
use_existing_python("/full/path/to/venvs/imfeatures/bin/python")

For a persistent setup, put both variables in ~/.Renviron:

IMFEATURES_SKIP_PYTHON=TRUE
RETICULATE_PYTHON=/full/path/to/venvs/imfeatures/bin/python

Install the Python packages into a cluster-managed module or virtual environment, not an automatically created R miniconda. At minimum the Python side needs Pillow and numpy; model backends add packages such as tensorflow/keras, torch, torchvision, thingsvision, resmem, and open-clip-torch.

The full HPC walkthrough is in:

vignette("hpc-setup", package = "imfeatures")
